The Unitar (one-string guitar) is an electric guitar with only one string, classed as a chordophone and associated with the American South. Home-made versions often take a piezoelectric sensor as pickup and need an external amplifier; the neck is often a PVC pipe, and no acoustic guitar-style soundbox is needed. It has appeared in Delta blues, and improvised folk instruments of the kind were popular in the 1930s and 1940s; its inventor Little Willie Joe Duncan also had a fair success in the 1950s with the rhythm-and-blues instrumental Twitchy.
共鳴方式簡潔而靈敏，音色變化主要依靠演奏者的滑音、顫音等技巧表現。與標準多弦吉他: The way it resonates is simple and sensitive, and the changes of timbre come mainly from the player's slides, vibrato and other techniques. Beside a standard multi-string guitar the one-string guitar sounds thinner but carries more, with something of the plaintive quality of a blues harmonica. Its timbre sits between an instrument and a voice, expressive and open to improvisation, and it suits the emotional tension and the storytelling of the blues especially well.

單弦吉他在美國音樂史上有著有趣的發展軌跡。密西西比州藍調音樂家埃迪「單弦」瓊斯在: The one-string guitar has an interesting trajectory in American music history. The Mississippi blues musician Eddie One-String Jones had some success in regional music circles, and the blues musician of the same generation Lonnie Pitchford also played a similar home-made instrument. By the 1950s the instrument's inventor, Little Willie Joe Duncan, had greater success in a contemporary style. His rhythm-and-blues instrumental Twitchy, recorded with René Hall's band, had considerable commercial success in the 1950s and became an important landmark in the instrument's history. These musicians' contributions show how the one-string guitar moved from a folk blues instrument to a professional studio instrument.
